You calculate contributor earnings every month, but routing those funds across borders is another headache entirely. Before you can automate this workflow, you must clearly define what is a royalty for your business model. Manual tax collection and missing W-9s will eventually slow down your entire process. Moving past manual payouts requires an automated system that actually works.


**TLDR:**


- A royalty compensates owners for the right to profit from their intellectual property.
- You must collect W-9s from US creators and report year-end payouts using 1099 tax forms.
- Mandatory KYC and KYB verification blocks bad actors before any payout money moves.
- The Dots API consolidates onboarding, TIN matching, and lowest-cost global payouts.


## What Is a Royalty?


When structuring contributor payouts, you need a precise answer to the question: what is a royalty? A royalty is a[compensation to the owner](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/royalty) of intellectual property or natural resources for the right to profit from that asset, such as a songwriter earning royalties each time their track streams. This legally binding[payout](https://usedots.com/blog/what-is-a-payout/) goes to an individual or company for the ongoing use of their work.

## Royalty Tax Obligations


Royalty earnings trigger distinct tax reporting obligations, including[foreign contractor withholding tax](https://usedots.com/blog/guide-to-us-tax-withholding-for-foreign-contractors/) rules. You must build an exact compliance workflow long before you disburse funds. For example, under[IRC §1441](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/nra-withholding) , payouts to foreign creators face a default 30% withholding tax unless they claim a reduced treaty rate. If your service disburses a $10,000 royalty batch without capturing the correct certification, you carry the $3,000 tax liability, not the creator.


When paying US-based creators, collect[W-9s](https://usedots.com/blog/what-is-irs-form-w-9-everything-you-need-to-know) (US tax identification forms) to verify taxpayer details. At year-end, report these payouts using[1099s](https://usedots.com/blog/businesses-guide-1099-contractors/) (tax forms for reporting non-employee compensation). Creators calculate this liability on 92.35%, and foreign entities may instead need to file a[W-8BEN-E form](https://usedots.com/blog/w-8ben-e-form-guide/) (foreign status certification forms).

Mandatory KYC (Know Your Customer) and KYB (Know Your Business) verification stops bad actors instantly, and foreign individual creators often must complete a[Form W-8BEN](https://usedots.com/blog/what-is-a-w-8ben-form/) (foreign status certification forms) to certify their status.


Knowing[which 1099 form to use for contractors](https://usedots.com/blog/which-1099-form-for-contractors/) matters here, and a developer-friendly API offers the best path forward. We built Dots to consolidate onboarding, TIN (Taxpayer Identification Number) matching,[1099-NEC vs 1099-MISC](https://usedots.com/blog/1099-nec-vs-misc-key-differences/) filings, and payouts under a single contract. Upfront TIN matching catches mismatches before any payout batch clears, acting as a structural defense against[IRS CP2100 notices](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/understanding-your-cp2100-or-cp2100a-notice) . Your team skips the manual paperwork while keeping disbursements flowing on schedule.


## Why a Royalty Matters in the Creator Economy


To scale your digital service, you must move beyond understanding what is a royalty. Distributing these earnings with precision determines whether you retain top contributors or lose them to competitors. Automated global payouts act as a direct competitive advantage.


Here are five reasons mastering this disbursement lifecycle matters:


- Creator retention: Contributors depend on predictable cash flow. Payment delays cause your best earners to migrate to competing services.
- Global rail access: Paying international creators requires deep local connectivity. We built Dots so it automatically routes each payout through the lowest-cost rail available for the recipient's jurisdiction, including for[music royalty payouts](https://usedots.com/solutions/music-royalties/) .
- Eliminating manual work: Processing earnings by hand creates immediate bottlenecks. Automated infrastructure bypasses this drag, letting your team focus on core product development instead of back-office paperwork. By moving identity verification and tax form collection to a unified API, you remove friction as your payee count scales. This end-to-end consolidation guarantees both compliance checks and fund routing execute instantly under one contract.
- Tax liability control: Missing certifications put the withholding bill on you, not the creator. On a $10,000 royalty batch to a foreign creator with no W-8BEN on file, you owe the $3,000 default 30% withholding. Collecting W-9s and W-8BENs at onboarding keeps that liability off your books.
- Fraud prevention: Royalty accounts attract fake payees who want to redirect earnings. KYC and KYB checks at onboarding verify each payee, and Dots screens every payee against global watchlists before funds move. Blocking a bad actor before the first payout is simpler than recovering money after it clears.


## Final Thoughts on Paying Your Creators


Retaining your talent requires reliable and fast cash flow. You need an automated system to route payments through local networks without delays.


Picture a mid-size creator service with 400 contributors spread across 30 countries. Each month your finance team used to spend days reconciling spreadsheets, chasing W-9s and W-8BENs, and manually calculating withholding before a single payout went out. With onboarding, TIN matching, and tax form collection consolidated under one contract, that same batch clears in hours instead of days, and your team spends that time on product work instead of paperwork.


Consider a songwriter in Germany earning streaming royalties and a freelance illustrator in Ohio earning licensing fees. The German creator files a W-8BEN to certify foreign status and claim a treaty rate, while the Ohio creator submits a W-9 so you can issue a 1099 at year-end. Mandatory KYC and KYB checks run for both before funds move, catching mismatched tax details or fraudulent accounts before they reach your payout rail. Routing each payment through the lowest-cost local rail for the recipient's country keeps more of each royalty in the creator's pocket, which is the detail that keeps top talent from migrating to a competing service.

## FAQ


### Stripe Connect vs Dots for paying royalties to international creators?


Dots routes funds across[190+ countries](https://docs.usedots.com/references/supported-countries/) using 300+ local rails, whereas Stripe Connect stops at[46 supported markets](https://stripe.com/global) . When paying international contributors, Dots settles funds over real-time networks without adding[Stripe's 1.5% instant-transfer surcharge](https://support.stripe.com/questions/what-are-instant-payouts-and-who-is-eligible) .


Consider a creator service paying a video editor in the Philippines and a musician in Brazil. Stripe Connect requires each recipient to set up a Stripe-supported bank account, which excludes many contributors in markets outside its 46 countries and pushes you toward slower wire transfers or third-party workarounds. Dots instead routes the Philippine payout through a local bank rail and the Brazilian payout through Pix, so both creators receive funds in local currency without an intermediary.


Onboarding also differs in practice. Stripe Connect typically requires you to build custom logic for collecting W-8BENs (foreign status certification forms) and matching TINs (Taxpayer Identification Numbers) across jurisdictions, while the Dots API bundles that KYC (Know Your Customer) and tax-form collection into one onboarding flow. For a service with contributors across 20 or more countries, this removes the need for separate compliance logic per region and keeps 1099 and W-8BEN-E recordkeeping under a single contract.


### Can I process a royalty payout through Dots without building my own KYC flow?


Yes. The Dots API includes a white-labeled onboarding portal that runs mandatory KYC and KYB verification checks before any money moves. This blocks bad actors instantly and eliminates the need for your engineering team to build custom identity screening tools.


### Should I use Tipalti or Dots to pay contributor royalties?


Dots typically settles funds over supported real-time rails through a developer-friendly API, while Tipalti relies on slower ACH-batch timing built for back-office finance spreadsheets. If you need to integrate fast, contributor-facing payouts directly into your service, Dots provides the better infrastructure.


Consider a music distribution service paying 5,000 songwriters a monthly royalty batch. With Tipalti, the finance team exports a payout file, maps vendor records, and waits for ACH settlement, a process built around accounts-payable workflows rather than contributor-facing disbursement. With Dots, the same batch routes through the API directly from your royalty calculation engine, pulling recipient bank details, tax status, and payout rail preference from a single onboarding record already captured during signup.


The distinction matters most at scale. A service onboarding new creators weekly needs KYC (Know Your Customer), W-9 collection, and 1099 generation tied to the same payout event, not a separate finance tool bolted onto a spreadsheet export. Dots consolidates that onboarding, tax form capture, and fund routing under one contract, so a songwriter in Lagos and one in Nashville both receive payouts through the rail best suited to their location without your engineering team maintaining custom logic for each country. Tipalti's architecture instead assumes a vendor-management model, which fits recurring supplier payments better than high-volume, contributor-facing royalty runs where onboarding speed and payout transparency drive retention.


### After you define what is a royalty for your creators, how does Dots handle the 1099 tax filing?


The Dots API handles the filing automatically based on your transaction logs. It collects W-9s during onboarding and runs upfront TIN matching, then generates and submits the 1099 forms at year-end so you skip the manual paperwork.
